system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2186-04-24 19:03:00 to 2186-04-25 18:06:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A male patient with hypogammaglobulinemia, mitochondrial myopathy, coronary artery disease, and orthostatic hypotension was admitted for scheduled inpatient IVIG infusion. He received premedication with IV fluids and Benadryl, and the infusion was administered slowly overnight due to his fluid sensitivity. During the infusion, he experienced mild chest discomfort and shortness of breath, which resolved with oxygen and rate reduction. He remained on telemetry and was observed overnight. The following day, he reported residual grogginess but improved mental clarity by afternoon. He was discharged home in stable condition with medication adjustments, including a switch to chewable aspirin, and plans for potential transition to outpatient IVIG. No acute complications occurred.
problems: Coronary atherosclerosis of unspecified type of vessel, native or graft

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in with chest pressure. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had this off and on for two days. Yesterday it was really bad—right in the center, lasted over an hour. I felt nauseous and was sweating a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And today you felt weak and dizzy, is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. My mouth was dry, and I just felt awful. My PCP told me to come in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good call. We’ve checked your heart enzymes and EKG. The good news is no sign of a heart attack. But your kidney function was a bit off—creatinine was up to 1.5, which is higher than your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. I’ve had that before when I’m dehydrated. I’ve been skipping my IV fluids because of the leg biopsies coming up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Your mitochondrial disease makes you more sensitive to dehydration, and that can trigger chest pain. We’re giving you 2 liters of IV fluids now to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my heart this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can’t rule it out completely, but your EKG showed only minor changes, and your enzymes stayed negative. Your cardiologist wants you to do a stress echo tomorrow to be sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You did the stress test this morning. I have the results—your heart function is normal, no signs of blockages or ischemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So what caused the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely, it was due to dehydration, which we know can worsen angina in your case. Your creatinine is already back down to 1.2 after the fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Plavix? I’ve been off it for five days for the biopsies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve restarted it. You’re back on all your usual meds—Plavix, aspirin, metoprolol, the works. We switched your aspirin to chewable again, same as last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. I remember that helped last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you today. You’re stable, pain-free, and labs look good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Should I restart my regular IV fluids at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. Staying hydrated is key, especially with your mitochondrial condition. Keep up with your appointments with your PCP and cardiologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll have your discharge papers ready soon. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. Any chest pain since this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: None at all. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Remember to take your meds as prescribed and follow up with your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ride is here. You’re cleared to go home. Call if you have any chest pain, dizziness, or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll stay on top of my fluids and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of mitochondrial myopathy, coronary artery disease, and orthostatic hypotension was admitted for evaluation of intermittent chest pressure over two days, associated with nausea and diaphoresis. Initial concerns for acute coronary syndrome were raised due to his cardiac history, but serial troponins were negative and EKG showed only transient ST depressions. A chest x-ray revealed no acute process, and an exercise stress echocardiogram showed normal left ventricular function with no evidence of inducible ischemia. His symptoms were attributed to dehydration, exacerbated by his mitochondrial disease, which also caused a transient rise in creatinine from baseline. He was treated with 2 liters of IV normal saline, restarted on clopidogrel after a 5-day hold, and continued on his baseline cardiac medications. His condition improved, and he was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to maintain hydration and follow up with his primary care physician and cardiologist.
